utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. You are continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Before I put questions to you, Mr. Zaric, I wish to inform the Trial Chamber of a small let's call it technical problem we have. Mr. Zaric's glasses have not been brought to him and he has not received his medicine for today. However, we have been assured that the security guards have gone to fetch these things, so that probably during the proceedings this issue will be resolved. If we have to introduce some documents into evidence, we will wait for Mr. Zaric to receive his glasses. That's all I wanted to inform the Trial Chamber about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah. It's unfortunate that there is this lapse. I hope that those concerned will make sure that this doesn't happen again. We would like to support Mr. Zaric so that he can give his evidence and complete it without a hitch. So we hope these matters will be received in due course. So you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, before the end of the session, we mentioned the arrival of volunteers to the village of Batkusa and your meeting with Mr. Nikolic, Lieutenant Nikolic, and Makso Simeunovic, and what they told you. Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic. Did Commander Nikolic tell you at that time under whose command these units were? Were they under the command of the 17th Tactical Group or under some other command?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In brief, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic told us that there had been a meeting on the 12th, in Donji Zabar, and that on that occasion Mr. Todorovic had told him that these policemen from Republika Srpska Krajina were under his control and that they would take care of this unit, that the unit would be supplied, organised, received, and accommodated by him, that he would organise all these things. And he said that Mr. Blagoje Simic was also present at the meeting, did not oppose this. From this, I concluded that this was a unit which had not arrived in order to join the 17th Tactical Group and become part of it. Let me just add that on the 13th, when we were going in the direction of Batkusa, at about 11.00 a.m. or 12.00 noon, Mr. Antic and I stopped briefly in Batkusa and received information from some local people that these special purpose units had stopped some buses, searched people, and taken foreign currency from some people. When we transmitted this information to Mr. Nikolic, I used a very vulgar expression. I said they were a sort of gang. I said: What kind of specials are these who can stop people and take their money? And he said something like this: That he had been given the information he had been given to us that he would do everything to keep this under a certain control and that he would monitor their behaviour. He said: Stay away from them. They will be accommodated in the area of the village of Obudovac. And with this comment of his, all discussion of these people ended, and that's all we every learned about who these people were who had arrived by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Mr. Zaric, what would your position -- what is your knowledge on the issue of whether these persons who arrived on the helicopters, whether we call them volunteers, specials, paramilitaries is neither here nor there, but what is your knowledge as to whether or not they were absorbed into the structure of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning, to be quite honest, I knew very little. I'm speaking of the first days and of the 13th, when I had a conversation with Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic on this topic. However, soon afterwards, I received reliable information, quite reliable, that these were people who had been specially trained not far from the town of Ilok, in a place called Pajsos and Sarengrad, and these camps had been organised to train policemen. From this, I drew the conclusion that this was a team, or rather, a camp, training special purpose policemen. I checked this information later on and had some conversations about this, and I hope that during my testimony we will come to these episodes, where I will talk about this topic in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric, on that point for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I had exactly the same question as Judge Williams, but I leave it for the cross-examination and hope that it will be clarified more in detail. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, have we rounded off this topic now? But could you tell us, all the same, where you received certain information about who these people were, who had sent them, and how they had arrived to the village of Batkusa.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most precise information about the arrival of this special purposes unit was given to me on the 9th of May, in Belgrade, in the building of the SSNO, or rather, in the administration of the security administration of the Yugoslav army, where I went on orders from my commander to inform the people in charge there of the massacre that had taken place on the 8th of May, 1992, in the village of Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you learn on that occasion in the SSNO, that is, the security organ?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does this mean I have to pass over the episode of Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, but now we are talking about these volunteers. What did you learn about them, just about them?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question. After providing this information as to what had happened in Crkvina, there was a very sharp verbal exchange between Colonel Maksimovic whom I knew from before as a security officer employed in the SSNO because he was born in the village of Obudovac in the municipality of Samac, and the general at the time who was in charge of the SSNO, Aleksandar Vasiljevic, also known as Aco. When Colonel Maksimovic put a question to General Vasiljevic as to what kind of people had gone there to Posavina and perpetrated such crimes, General Vasiljevic responded, and General Gligorevic was also present, and at that time he was the deputy head of the security administration, which means that he was General Aleksandar Vasiljevic's deputy. He said something like this: Colonel Maksimovic, do you think that I should go there to liquidate that gang, or should the person who sent them there deal with them? This response by General Vasiljevic prompted Colonel Maksimovic to ask: General, I don't know who sent those people to Posavina and Bosanski Samac. Then General Vasiljevic said, very briefly to Gligorevic: Please bring that document -- order that document to be brought here to the office. Very soon after that, General Gligorevic called someone up on the telephone, and an officer arrived, brought in a document, and immediately left that office. On that piece of paper, which I personally saw in that office, was a request from the government of the municipality of Samac, addressed to the command of the RV and PVO of Yugoslavia, that is, their security services, asking for the use of helicopters in order to transport special purpose units that had been trained together in the area of Ilok, and this had been organised by the security service of the RV and PVO, the aviation of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, let's clarify these abbreviations you have used. What does RV and PVO mean?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means military air force, and PVO means anti-aircraft defence. This is a special entity or segment within the armed forces of the army of -- the armed forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it was always treated as a special entity, a separate entity, within the armed forces of the socialist Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So you are saying that this was one branch of the military?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you slow down so that the interpreters can keep up.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you see on this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was signed by the president of the Executive Board of the Serbian municipality of Samac, Mr. Mirko Jovanovic. However, Mr. Maksimovic, Colonel Maksimovic, said that he could not decipher anything in that signature and that he was convinced that the document had been signed for Jovanovic by Mr. Stevan Todorovic. As I also saw the signature, where it says "for," in front of the name of the president of the Executive Board Mirko Jovanovic, and afterwards I saw Mr. Todorovic's signature on other documents. I really did think that this signature resembled that of Mr. Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. I'd just like to ask Mr. Zaric one question. At that point in time, Mr. Zaric, when you saw this document with the -- signed on behalf of Mr. Jovanovic, at that period in time when you saw the document, had you ever seen Mr. Todorovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up to that moment, I had not seen it. Up to that moment, I hadn't seen it. I looked at the document. I know what Mirko Jovanovic means. Sometimes it's very hard to decipher short signatures, by anyone. But when I remember that document and the way it was signed, and then, when I bring back to my memory other documents I saw that were signed by Mr. Todorovic, then it really seems to me that it was Mr. Todorovic who signed it. This testimony of mine cannot be taken as meaning that I'm a hundred per cent certain that it was Mr. Todorovic's signature, but based on Maksimovic's comment and what I saw, I drew this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. Is it possible that the document in question could be produced? Is it in the possession of anybody or has it been destroyed or burnt or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, since I was trying very, very hard to find this document and used all my efforts, not only my efforts, but efforts of our investigators and everyone, we couldn't reach this document. This document was mentioned in Mr. Zaric's interview earlier, and we knew about the existence of this document. I even tried military security organs to get reach to this document, but unfortunately no luck. Our information, the last information in respect to this document, was that during NATO shelling of Belgrade, part of the archive of the military organs was destroyed and this document -- not just this. There was another very important document that Mr. Zaric made during that meeting, and we -- this is the other document that I was looking for, but unfortunately there was no luck and we couldn't find this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know Mirko Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to discuss this document with Mirko Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Mirko Jovanovic tell you in connection with this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Jovanovic told me, very decidedly, that he had no idea that people were going from the Samac area to receive that training, nor did he know of any signature or any document with the contents I have mentioned. He said he never wrote or signed anything resembling that document and the contents of the document about which I testified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Do you know anything about the connections between Mr. Stevan Todorovic and people in the command of the air force and the anti-aircraft defence?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us what you know and how you came by this knowledge.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first knowledge that Mr. Todorovic had special connections with the people from the air force and the anti-air defence of Yugoslavia came directly from him. I heard this from him in early April, in Samac, during a conversation where he found me sitting in a cafe and wanted to have a brief chat with me. To paraphrase very briefly this part of our conversation, he wanted me to go with him to Belgrade, to the command of the Yugoslav air force and anti-air defence, to be introduced to some eminent and important officers of the JNA, and he said: I hope you won't mind that they have a rather pro-Chetnik orientation and they have links to Mr. Seselj and the Radicals. And I said that the two of us had nothing further to say about that topic. I said I wasn't interested in those kind of people and that I wasn't interested in their connections with the Radicals, and that's how I know -- or rather, conclude that Mr. Todorovic had already established contacts with people from this important unit within the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion later on to find out about his close connections with these people?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and this was in late May, after the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, Colonel Mico Djurdjevic, was replaced, when we went together to a meeting in the air force and anti-air defence of Yugoslavia, Mr. Blagoje Simic, Mr. Stevan Todorovic, Mr. Miroslav Tadic, Mr. Milos Bogdanovic, and I. It was then that I saw very cordial and intimate relations between Mr. Todorovic and the most responsible people in the command of the air force and anti-air defence of Yugoslavia, who were present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We'll discuss this meeting later on. Just tell me: Who were these people who were the most responsible?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the air force and anti-air defence of Yugoslavia, General Bajic, Colonel Jeremic, who was in charge of security, one of the most responsible people for security in the air force. The only one who was not present at that meeting was General Stevanovic, who at that time held the post of commander of air force and anti-air defence of Yugoslavia. He did not attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. We'll come to that meeting. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, before we leave this meeting, what was the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you remember the exact date? You said it was in late May. Can you remember approximately what the date of that meeting in Belgrade was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't. However hard I try, I can't remember the precise date. But it was towards the very end of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But Your Honours, I really cannot remember the exact date at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Late May is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, we'll move on from this topic. I'll ask you some questions, to which I would like you to give very brief replies, about what you know about the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA. What can you say about the establishment of the 17th Tactical Group, whether it was a part of any unit, where the command was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA, in organisational terms, began in the autumn of 1991. I can't be precise about the date. When I say "autumn," I mean October or November 1991. According to its organisation, it was linked to the 17th Corps of the JNA, whose headquarters was in Tuzla and whose commander was General Savo Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where was the command, or rather, this 17th Corps with the headquarters in Tuzla was under whose command?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 17th Corps of the Yugoslav People's Army was linked to the 2nd military district, and its seat was in Sarajevo and its commander was General Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. Could you, in order to have a more precise picture of the situation, could you tell us something about the manpower of the 17th Tactical Group and what kind of arms they were having. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: His Honour has some questions concerning the 17th Tactical Group. But before that, I'd like to ask Mr. Zaric: And who was this military district responsible to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd military district was responsible to the chief -- to the Main Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army, with its seat in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Tell us, please: Where was the command of the 17th Tactical Group of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the 17th Tactical Group of the Yugoslav People's Army was in the village of Pelagicevo, which was in the territorial sense was part of the municipality of Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who commanded the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA and who were members of that command?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the commander of the 17th Tactical Group was Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic. I know that the chief of the staff of the 17th Tactical Group was Major Brajkovic. I know that the head of artillery was Mr. Sabrija, I can't remember his last name right now but he was of Muslim ethnicity. He was chief of artillery at the 17th Tactical Group. I know that the duty of the commander of the security and intelligence service was performed by Mr. Marko Simeunovic. People who worked in the rear and who was involved with personnel affairs and who were in the command, I know those people by sight, but I cannot recall their first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you tell us, of course, if you know: Where was the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group, and could you tell us its size, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 17th Tactical Group had an area of responsibility which was relatively large. It covered the area of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, northward, a part of the municipality of Modrica in a westerly direction, part of the municipality of Gradacac to the south, part of the municipality of Orasje again in a northerly direction and part of the Brcko municipality in the easterly direction. So several municipalities or, rather, I'd say parts of various municipalities which I have just listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Where did the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group and in relation to the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group, if we're talking about the town of Samac, was -- to do with the right bank of the Bosna River, that is, from the mouth of the Bosna downstream towards the village of Zasavica. So that is the so-called western area. In the north, it was part of -- a part of the right bank of the Sava River, right up to the bridge across the Sava, extended to the village of Tursinovac, which is then linked with Grebnice, which was not in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I'm getting your meaning, the village of Prud, which was part of the municipality of Samac, was -- and which is on the left bank of the Bosna River, wasn't in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It wasn't. And several villages of Croat ethnicity which had more ties with the municipality of Orasje and at that time were part of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Counsel, is Mr. Zaric going to answer my questions or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now these questions -- yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: And in addition, when Mr. Zaric spoke about the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group, if I understood him well, that means that the 17th Tactical Group, under the command of Mr. Nikolic, included, as to ethnicity, Serbs, in the centre; and Muslims, in the south; and what about the western part of that area? Could you also respond to those questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, which units made the 17th Tactical Group? What was their purpose? What kind of armaments did they have? And how strong was the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To make it quite clear, I'd rather speak about the final stages of the establishment of the 17th Tactical Group, because I presume that would be easier for us to understand it. So I'd rather not talk about early days. I'm talking about the 17th Tactical Group on the eve of the conflict. And let me answer the previous question of His Honour. The 17th Tactical Group at that time was six to seven thousand men strong. If we are talking about the number of soldiers who were in the 17th Tactical Group. Now, as far as I know, the 17th Tactical Group embraced five infantry battalions, and two artillery units. I'm not quite sure what they were called, but they were also part of the 17th Tactical Group. One of such units had been transferred to the area of Loncari, that is, towards Brcko, and one part of that unit was stationed more to the south, near the village of Slatina. So that in addition to these five infantry detachments, to call them that, and these units, there were also a police company, a signals company, but they were staff units of the command of the 17th Tactical Group. And the overall strength, I've already said it, I'd say it was between six and seven thousand men altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And tell us, Mr. Zaric, what kind of armaments did the 17th Tactical Group have at its disposal, if you know that? What kind of infantry weapons, what kind of artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All infantry battalions, that is, detachments, in the early days, before the army of Republika Srpska was formed, they were called detachments. They were armed only with light infantry weapons. That means automatic rifles, all sorts of automated, hand-held launchers, hand grenades, and the ammunition that goes with that kind of weaponry. The rest, that is, the artillery units, well, one was a tank unit. There was a Howitzer unit. There were also 110 unit, these are the 110-millimetre guns and 100-millimetre recoilless guns, technically called Zis, Z-i-s. So there were several types of artillery weapons. And as for the combat armoured vehicles, apart from tanks -- apart from tanks, as combat armoured vehicles, there were also the so-called Pragas and combat armoured vehicles, CAV, in contrast with the tanks, they have rubber tyres and are more mobile. They are more easily manoeuvreable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And the last question that was asked by His Honour Judge Lindholm was: What was the ethnic composition in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd really not try to give any exact figure as to the ethnic composition at the level of the 17th Tactical Group as a whole. I could give you a very precise information as to the ethnic composition of the 4th Detachment, where I was assistant commander and where my area of responsibility and work was. But generally speaking, at the level of the 17th Tactical Group, there were people of all ethnic groups, no doubt, but again, no doubt the majority were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, in the territory which was in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group, were the places inhabited by Serbs, Croats, and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, we shall now go back to the 4th Detachment, and I'd like to ask you, since we already heard a great deal about the 4th Detachment, to try to be as brief as possible. Can you tell us how the 4th Detachment was replenished?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the mobilisation call-ups through the municipal secretariat for National Defence, that is how this unit called the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army was replenished. That is, from the territory of the neighbourhood community of Samac, or rather, from the -- to be more precise, from the territory of the town of Samac. All the military conscripts which were -- who were fit for combat, who had volunteered and responded to the call-up, they all went to the secretariat for National Defence, would then receive the summons and then sent to the command of the 4th Detachment and then assigned by our command to subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what can you tell us about the internal organisation of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment was made of the command, comprising the commander, his deputy assistant for intelligence and security, assistant commander for logistics, operations officer in the command, and in terms of formation, the reconnaissance unit, the signals unit, and the medical unit were also attached to it. Likewise, the 4th Detachment comprised four infantry companies, and every infantry company had several platoons as subordinate units, and these platoons, in their turn, had groups of ten soldiers as the lowest mobile unit in the 4th Detachment as a larger unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did all these organisational units that you've just mentioned have their commanders or heads from the company commander to the detachment commander?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them, all the posts were filled, and everybody knew exactly who is the company commander, who is the platoon commander, who is the company commander, who is the squad commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: These small units, these squads that you mentioned, that is, the reconnaissance unit, the medical unit, when were they activated?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The medical and reconnaissance units were activated when the hostilities broke out on the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Who commanded the reconnaissance unit?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reconnaissance unit was commanded by Mr. Fadil Topcagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And who commanded the medical unit?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The medical unit was commanded by Dr. Mirko Sisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned here the signals unit. Who commanded that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Its commander was Radovan Djuric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Right. What was the ethnic composition of the 4th Detachment, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the eve of the hostilities, I remember rather well that the 4th Detachment was over 450 men strong. In that detachment, there were slightly over 250 Serbs, 154 Muslims, and 44 were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were members of all the ethnic groups assigned to command posts, be it companies, platoons, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just corroborate it with a fact. In the detachment command, a very important post was the command operations officers, and that duty was conducted by Mehmed Vukovic. Mr. Celikovic commanded the 1st company, Andrija Jasenica commanded the 2nd company. The 3rd company was commanded with Naser Ramusovic and the commander of the 4th company was Mr. Vlado Sisic. Mr. Andra Jasenica and Mr. Naser Ramusovic are individuals of Croat ethnicity [as interpreted]. And for instance, we had a platoon commander, Hasan Ibralic, called Djuro, Tadija Brandic, who is Croat, Anto Becic who is of Croat ethnicity. So that from this listed roster of names, one could conclude that in the command of the 4th Detachment, all three ethnic groups were represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. But I will ask you once again to slow down. I do not know whether I heard you well, but let me just check the transcript. If I heard you properly, you said Andra Jasenica. Do you mean Dzemal Jasenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. It is Mr. Dzemal Jasenica, whose nickname is Andra. And since we all call him that, I got carried away by his nickname rather than by his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And there is another thing which is not correct in the transcript. Perhaps you said that. Dzemal Jasenica, called Andra, is of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dzemal Jasenica, called Andra, is of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, how were the members of the 4th Detachment issued with weapons and other gear? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please return to his microphone.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following the 5th of January, and the adoption of the decision to form the 4th Detachment as a unit of the Yugoslav People's Army, in March -- no, in February and March, we held two drills, two training exercises, which took place in Potocari, which is in the territory of the Brcko municipality. Otherwise, this place is known as the training grounds of the Yugoslav People's Army for the -- as a shooting range where infantry weapons are -- where shooting from infantry weapons is practiced. After this exercise, to which we went by buses, on that occasion, the logistics service of the 17th Tactical Group distributed weapons to the members of the 4th Detachment, with the accompanying documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did the members of the 4th Detachment get on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards personal weapons, they were issued with automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles, M-48, if I may call it that. These are rather old rifles. Automatic weapon 756. These are those black German automatic weapons, if I may call them that. Hand-held launchers and hand-held machine-guns. This was the basic armament that was issued to the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of gear were the members of the 4th Detachment issued with?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were issued with uniforms, but not all of them, because at that time there weren't enough uniforms available. But those that the logistics had at its disposal was distributed amongst the men, and by and large it was the conventional old uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army which we in our lingo called SMB olive-green/grey uniform. So SMB.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you issued with anything else?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the rifle, everybody was issued with a combat kit, and this is a small cotton pouch with four frames of ammunition. Of them, two were empty and two were full. And everyone of these frames contained 30 bullets. They were also issued with a certain number of masks. There weren't enough masks for everybody, but those that they had distributed and also they were issued with bandages and the basic things for the first aid and then a small hose to dig trenches, I mean other kind of a tool that any army will use under peacetime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the 4th Detachment keep a record of its members?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did it keep a record of what the members of the 4th Detachment were issued with, I mean gear, ammunition, weapons, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully and completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was there any order or some instruction for the members of the 4th Detachment about the need to look after the gear and weapons that they were issued with?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of -- the Chief of Staff, Brajkovic, had issued such a command, and during the exercises which I mentioned, and I mentioned two of them that took place in February and March, 1992, during one of those exercises, Commander Lieutenant Nikolic was present too, and one of those exercises was also present by the Chief of Staff, Mr. Brajkovic. They, in addition to an instruction in writing, how was one to look after weapons safely, how the weapons were to be handled and treated, they also issued some oral instructions as to how one should treat those weapons, that they should keep them away from homes, avoid any possibility of some excesses, and it was prohibited to carry weapons in the street or anywhere else unless very strict order to that effect had been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did it happen that members of the 4th Detachment failed to comply with these instructions and the order?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were two such instances. Professionally -- no, let me not put it that way, but let's say ex officio, my task was to monitor the conduct of the members of the 4th Detachment in relation to the weapons they had been issued with. We had two cases when two members -- I remember that one's name was Mikerevic and the other one was called Antic. One, during a wedding, and another one during, I believe, one of the religious holidays, came out into a yard and fired a whole round from that automatic weapon. And when I was notified about this, I put together a written report. I notified Mr. Makso Simeunovic, and believe me that a day or two after they had received my report, the military police turned up. They came from Pelagicevo, because they were attached to the command of the 17th Tactical Group, and weapons were seized from both those members of the 4th Detachment and disciplinary measures were applied to those two members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, please tell us: Where was the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the decision on mobilisation and the requisitioning of the building that we received from the municipal secretariat for National Defence, the 4th Detachment was stationed in the offices of the Samac textile industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many rooms were you given in the Samac textile industry?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were given two rooms. One was rather large and had a large conference table. About ten of us could sit around the table. And there was another smaller room where our operative officers were accommodated, and they had the radio set in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did this 4th Detachment have a depot or a warehouse where they housed the ammunition and weapons?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any depots or warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You've just told us that you had in the small room an operative officer and people who operated the communication equipment. So what kind of communication equipment did you have in the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were only charged with one radio set. That was a RUP 12 radio set. That's what we call it. This radio set weighs 12 kilogrammes, approximately, with all the accompanying accessories, and its range without relay was 12 kilometres. In addition to this radio set, we also had a sub-relay station, which was an integral part of this equipment, and owing to that sub-relay station, we could communicate with units a hundred kilometres away from Samac, if there was a need for such communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you use the radio set for, the RUP 12 radio set that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That radio set was used for communication between the 4th Detachment and the command of the 17th Tactical Group, i.e., their communications centre that they had in Pelagicevo, and it wasn't used for any other purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you, from the 4th Detachment, that is, the communications officers of the 4th Detachment, were you in the position to have -- to establish communication with other parts of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never established any contact with any other unit, apart from the command of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a telephone line in the command?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had a regular telephone line and we had a telephone line, a direct line with the command in Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, because of your answer, something has not been translated very precisely. There was a telephone line in the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The regular telephone line?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a regular telephone line in the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have just one telephone number?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just one telephone, in the larger of the two rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment, was it ever lined up, publicly and introduced to the general public?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to talk about what happened in Potocari during the drill, then I could say that there we were the real army, that we were lined up, and that we were standing still while our commanders were talking to us and while we were practicing firing from the infantry weapons. But, having said that, I also need to say that the 4th Detachment was never lined up publicly, never paraded around the town of Samac, never from its establishment to the outbreak of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, the 4th Detachment, as a unit, was it always together as a group of people? Did it have barracks where it was accommodated?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 4th Detachment did not have its barracks, nor it had a barracks life, so to say. It did not have any such activities that would require its special organisation. People lived normally, they led normal lives, up to the outbreak of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say that people led normal lives, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is that the 4th Detachment was just -- existed just on paper, as far as its members are concerned, they would go to their companies, if they worked, or they would go to factories if they worked in factories. Those who were farmers, they would work their land. Those who had hobbies or were pensioners would engage in those hobbies. So this is what I meant by normal, every day life, the life of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that they lived in their family houses and apartments?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did members of the 4th Detachment receive any remuneration for their engagement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't receive any remuneration, nor was there any reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And the members of the command, were they paid for their duties?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not paid. They would meet only occasionally, and all of their activity boiled down to that. All of them had their normal, regular, every day activities that they continued performing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In front of the building where the command was -- of the 4th Detachment was, was there any sort of an insignia or something to mark that command?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some insignia from before. There were flag posts in front of that building, and on those flag posts, as of the 5th of January, we put up the flag of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and a flag of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These were the only symbols, the only parts of the iconography that we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, in 1992, before the outbreak of hostilities, did the 4th Detachment engage in any military patrols? Were they members of military patrols?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell us what patrols were those.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were patrols which were in order to observe the area. The main task of those patrols was to make runs of the suburbs of the town, especially the defence trenches on the right bank of the Bosna River and on the right bank of the Sava River, southwards down the railway line, along the silos, and then towards these, towards the Sava River, that is, towards the bridge on the Sava River. So the whole borderline area was patrolled and observed by the 4th Detachment members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have some small misunderstanding here. I believe that the translation was not accurate. On page 25, line 22, here it says: "Especially the defence trenches on the right bank of Sava," and Mr. Zaric was referring to embankments on the right side of the River Sava. Because there were no trenches at the time, particularly not defence trenches made at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure counsel can go over that with the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Can I have some more water, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher will assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, are you feeling well?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm feeling well, but my throat is a bit dry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So we may continue?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify this situation here. You were talking about embankments or dikes, weren't you? And what are those borderline areas along the right bank of the River Bosna and the right bank of the River Sava? In the translation it says you mentioned trenches, but what did you actually mean?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't mean trenches. I was talking about dikes or embankments protecting the town from the waters of the River Bosna and of the waters -- from the waters of the River Sava. So these are the dikes that had been erected a long time ago to protect the town from the high waters of the two rivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please tell us: Who was -- who appointed people to those patrols?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the commanders of companies or commander of squads in those areas that they were in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And who did their patrols report to after the end of the patrol?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They reported to the commander of the 4th Detachment, to the deputy commander or possibly to the duty operations officer in the command who was on duty at that time. But in principle, all the information finally reached the commander or his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the patrols had the authority to use weapons in certain given circumstances during those patrols?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was strictly forbidden to them by the command of the 17th Tactical Group and by the commander Antic. Those patrols were usually during the night; during the day there was no reason whatsoever for them to patrol, and they were strictly forbidden to use weapons, regardless of any possible situation that they might come across.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Just another question about these patrols. Do you know if these patrols of the 4th Detachment were patrolling on the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. There were such patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to go back to another topic that we have already touched upon. You have already said, Mr. Zaric, that you participated in a number of meetings of the coordination body of the local commune of Bosanski Samac, and you've also told us that when this coordination body had been set up. Can you now tell us whether you were a member of this coordination body.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not its member, but I was invited to its meetings regularly, and in agreement with my commander, Antic, since I was also an assistant commander for morale and information, I would respond to the invitation of that coordination body that invited me whenever they thought that my presence was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In what capacity did you attend those meetings of the coordination body of the local commune of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the capacity of the assistant for morale and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who did you represent on any such occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I represented the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you attend all the meetings or only the meetings to which you were invited?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended only those meetings to which I was invited by the secretary of this coordination body or its president, Mr. Hadzialijagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you attended those meetings, who usually chaired those meetings?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More often than not, the chairperson of those meetings was Mr. Safet Hadzialijagic, also known as Pop.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what post did Mr. Hadzialijagic hold in the local commune?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was the president of the council of the local commune of the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you discuss at the meetings that you attended?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the most topical issue was always security. We also touched upon the political situation, but it was usually the security problems in the town of Samac and its vicinity that we discussed. We discussed the things that were going on and that was the major topic of our discussions. The chief of the public security station was always there. There was also the secretary for National Defence, the Chief of Staff, and people from the political life of the town were also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The patrols by the 4th Detachment, through the suburbs of the town, was that ever discussed at any of the meetings of the coordination body of the local commune?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: What kind of an agreement was reached about those patrols?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed that body about the need which stemmed from our security intelligence for the members of the 4th Detachment to patrol these suburbs, suburban areas, in the interest of all the citizens of Samac, given a number of the incidents that had taken place in town and its vicinity. I would also like to say that we got the green light from that coordination body, and also this coordination body agreed that patrols would be organised in addition to the police patrols and the SDA patrols. That is how the role of the 4th Detachment was ratified, and also that's how the role of the patrols of the SDA was ratified, by this coordination body.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you attend the meeting of the coordination body of the local commune of Bosanski Samac which was held on the 16th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you invited to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived at the meeting around 1830 hours, although the beginning of that meeting was at 1800 hours, but I was some half an hour late, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Why were you late arriving at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon, on the 16th of April, I was in Trnjak, visiting my mother, and I was helping her there with some chores. And at the moment when I was ready to leave to go to Samac, at that moment a delegation came in two cars. Some seven or eight people from Prud came to my mother's house, to its courtyard. And these people held me in a conversation, and we're talking about some security problems that had arose on that part of the Bosna where Prud is and where my native village is and where Mr. Cavka's paramilitaries from Croatia had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, Mr. Zaric: Who attended that meeting? Or to be more precise, in addition to the members of the council of the local commune, were there also representatives of some political party; and if so, which parties were they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in addition to the council members, there were also representatives of political parties, of the Reformists, of the SDP. I believe that there was also a representative of the Radical Party. And for the first time ever at any of these meetings, there were also -- there was also Mr. Marko Bozanovic and Mr. Alija Fitozovic. In addition to the representatives of political parties, there was also Mr. Sulejman Tihic, on behalf of the SDA; there was also Mr. Dragan Lukac, who already then had been appointed as the chief of the public security station in Bosanski Samac. He was the acting chief at that time. There was also Mr. Izet Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What about the representatives of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Evic was present at that meeting. I'm sure that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what about the Serbian Democratic Party representatives? Were they also there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they were not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what did you discuss at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Safet Hadzialijagic, in his capacity as the chairman of the coordination body, or the leader of that coordination body, informed all of us who were present that for the first time ever the meeting is attended by the newly appointed leaders of the new Territorial Defence, or to be more precise, leaders of the new staff of the Territorial Defence of Samac municipality. He mentioned the names of Mr. Marko Bozanovic, as the staff commander, and Alija Fitozovic as the chief of that new staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what was the reaction of other participants in the meeting when they heard that information? I would primarily be interested in you telling us what political parties and their representatives supported the newly established Territorial Defence and the newly appointed officials of the Territorial Defence or its staff.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the politicians voiced their comment, the floor was first taken by the new command of the territorial staff, Mr. Marko Bozanovic, who put us in the picture, so to say. He told us that he was officially appointed by the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as the commander of the Territorial Defence of Samac municipality, and that a similar decision was issued to Mr. Fitozovic, as the Chief of Staff, and that their nomination had been established at a meeting on the 13th of April. This was a joint meeting of the HDZ and the SDA parties in Grebnice, and it was pursuant to that agreement and pursuant to that proposal that the decision was issued and the new staff was officially established. When Mr. Bozanovic provided us with that explanation, the representatives of the Reformists and of the SDP, of Radicals as well as, and I don't know whether the Liberals were also there, I'm not sure, those are the people more familiar with the parliamentarian life and the way officials are appointed, they raised the question as to how it was possible to issue a decision on the appointment of the leaders of the Territorial Defence staff and the Chief of Staff without the approval of the Assembly and in the absence of the Serbian people, because nobody was present there on behalf of the Serbian Democratic Party or people who at that time represented the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. His simple reply was as follows: Mr. Tihic said something along these lines: Even if we had invited the Serbs to that meeting in Grebnice, we assume that they would not have come. That's why we issued this decision. Mr. Tihic said: We know that this is not really a legitimate decision, but that's what we decided because you Serbs have opted for the Yugoslav People's Army. This was a discussion that ensued after the information we received by the appointment of these people as the commander and the Chief of Staff respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that it is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We continue. Before we start, the Trial Chamber has been informed that actually the doctor had said that Mr. Simo Zaric no longer needs the medication. That's why it was not given to him. But we understand that the glasses have been brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I was informed by Mr. Zaric, he was to have received the medication. However, this is not important now. What matters is that his glasses have been brought to him, so there is no obstacle to his testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, before the break we were talking about the meeting of the coordination body of the Bosanski Samac local commune which was held in 1992, on the 13th of April. Can you tell us whether any proposals were made by the newly elected commander of the TO staff Bosanski Samac, Mr. Bozanovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a proposal. Mr. Marko Bozanovic immediately provided the information that for two days they had already been carrying out certain activities as new people in the TO staff. And at the coordination body, he informed us that practically all local communes were inhabited by Croats, or rather, all those local communes that were inhabited by Croats had agreed to have their units join the new TO staff and that according to his information, the new staff of the TO had about 1.600 men on their records and that they also had a written report from the Party of Democratic Action that the self-organised detachment - that's how they referred to it. It was the first time I had heard of them having a detachment - and he said that they had over 800 people who had joined the Territorial Defence from the town, and he sent a request, or rather, he addressed me directly with the following request. He said: Mr. Zaric, it would be a good thing if everything were done for the members of the 4th Detachment to join the new staff and the new Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you take part in the discussion at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and later on I made some comments with Mr. Tihic and Alija Fitozovic. And to the question put to me by the new commander, Marko Bozanovic, I replied that this was the first time I had heard that a Territorial Defence staff had been formed in Samac. I said that I knew that the 4th Detachment was part of the JNA and that I had no authority, as the assistant commander for security and intelligence, or for morale and information tasks, to say on behalf of the JNA that the 4th Detachment could now join the new TO. I told him that I would inform the commander of the 17th Tactical Group of all this and that I would try very soon to give him some feedback as to what the command of the JNA thought of the newly arisen situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Alija Fitozovic say anything, and did you have any exchanges with him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Alija and Mr. Izo arrived at the meeting drunk. That's not so important. But Mr. Alija Fitozovic said to me: Mr. Zaric, you may be surprised that 800 people from the town of Samac have already joined the Territorial Defence and that there are over 80 Serbs among them. I only said: Mr. Fitozovic, I recognise this sort of negative propaganda, and I know that it is now part of what's going on. But I said I had no authority to express any position on this. And when I -- after I had spoken to my command, I would be able to inform them of what the command of the 17th Tactical Group thought about this. I think that Mr. Fitozovic then came out with some data that was completely unconvincing, and I answered him in the way I have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zaric. How did this meeting end? Were any conclusions adopted?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No conclusions were adopted at that meeting, and the meetings of this organisational body were characterised by the fact that conclusions were never binding upon anyone, nor were they precise enough, and they were never actually implemented by anyone. I undertook to inform them, and they in effect had informed the coordination body that the new TO staff, under a new leadership, had been established. After this, we all went home, and it was about 10.00 p.m. when the meeting ended. And there were no binding conclusions that were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you undertook to inform the command of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA of the proposals made by the commander of the new Territorial Defence staff, Mr. Marko Bozanovic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. And I've just remembered something that Mr. Alija Fitozovic said. He said: Mr. Zaric, we have received weapons. We are publicly distributing weapons to our members. We are not doing anything surreptitiously. We started distributing these weapons yesterday. And this was the first time I had learned of this piece of information. I heard it from Mr. Fitozovic at the meeting of this coordination body.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that the meeting ended at about 2200 hours. Where did you go after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the meeting, I went to the command, and there I found only Mr. Antic of the members of the command. He was in charge of communications. And there were some people there who were getting ready to go on a patrol, and they had dropped in at the command. And very briefly, I told Commander Nikolic [as interpreted], and not concealing it from anyone else, what the upshot of the meeting had been. I told them what was going on, and he said: Tomorrow we have to inform Commander Nikolic of this and see what his position is. After this, I went to have a drink in a neighbouring cafe with a neighbour of mine, Mr. Vidak Prusina, and I stayed there perhaps half an hour after this conversation in the command. So I stayed with Vidak and had a drink with him for about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. On page 36, line 19, it reads: "I told Commander Nikolic." Shouldn't it be Antic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was just going to clarify this with Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You said that in the command of the 4th Detachment, you said this to Commander Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was Antic. He was the only one from the command whom I found there. If I said Nikolic, it was a slip of the tongue. I meant Commander Antic, the command of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. And when did you return home?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could have been about 11.00 p.m., about 2300 hours, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And who did you find in your flat?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found my wife and my sons, Denis and Mirel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you do after you came home?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told them an anecdote that I had heard from my neighbour, Vidak Prusina. He was a man who dabbled in astrology. So we broached the topic and he said: Zaric, you will go down in history in a bad way. And it seems to be coming true. But anyway, I told them about this, and then my wife first served dinner for me and told me that before I came home, someone had called her on the phone but didn't want to introduce himself. He simply rang up, and when she picked up the receiver, the person hung up. Maybe somebody wanted to check whether we were at home. I don't know. But this was actually nothing unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Later on that night, did you have any phone calls?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we went to bed, around midnight, the telephone rang, and my wife said: Oh, this must be for you, or maybe it's a provocation. When I picked up the receiver, it was the duty policeman in the public security station, Mr. Luka Gregurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you talk about with Mr. Luka Gregurevic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that Mr. Lukac, the chief, was right next to him and that he wanted to ask me something and say something to me. So I continued the conversation with Mr. Dragan Lukac, who was in the duty officer's room in the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did Dragan Lukac tell you on that occasion, the chief of the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan told me that a short while before, on his way back from Hrvatska Tisina, because he was driving Marko Bozanovic home from that meeting, that he saw, in Srpska Tisina, a soldier on the crossroads when one comes out of Hrvatska Tisina, in the direction of Srpska Tisina, and that he saw that he had a white band on his lapel. So he wanted to see what this meant. He noticed a soldier with a white band standing at night on a crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you reply?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said: Dragan, this is not my area of responsibility, but I could ring up some people I know to check. And if I get any information, I'll let you know. He asked me to do that, and I undertook to do that, and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you call someone after this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I rang up Mr. Stanko Djurdjevic, who had been a schoolmate of mine, and he was one of the directors of the Uniglas factory in Samac. And I asked him if he could tell me anything, because a soldier had been noticed at a crossroads with a white band on, and so on. And Stanko said to me: Are you calling me at this time of night for that? They may be having an exercise. I'll talk with you in the morning. As far as I know, there's nothing special going on. When Stanko told me this, I called the station right away, and Luka Gregurevic replied and said that the chief had already left to go home by car. I said to Luka: If you can speak to the chief, tell him that I talked to Stanko Djurdjevic and that Stanko said that one should not make a fuss about this, because it's possible that one of the units was having an exercise. And that was the end of that story with the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Just to clarify one thing. It might be translation or it might not. On page 38, line 16, Mr. Zaric says: "He saw that he had a white band on his lapel." I just want to check that Mr. Zaric did use the word "lapel." Or maybe, Mr. Zaric, you can answer me directly. Did you use the word "lapel"? You were talking about -- well, you say that Dragan told me that a short while before, et cetera, that he saw in Srpska Tisina a soldier on the crossroads, et cetera, and he saw that he had a white band on his lapel. I just want to check that "lapel" is the correct word in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. You understood correctly. That's what I was referring to. And Dragan said that the soldier was wearing some sort of military jacket. And when there was a gust of wind, because it was quite windy that night, he noticed that when his jacket moved, there was a white band hanging from his epaulette. So yes, you observed that correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. That's just to clarify, then. It was an epaulette, not a lapel, in English. Maybe you could just point to where an epaulette would be, Mr. Zaric, if you could, just to make sure. Because in English there is a difference between an epaulette and a lapel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To me it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, in B/C/S maybe it is. But could you just point to where on a soldier's uniform an epaulette would be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be from this part of the shoulder to the end. Practically this is what there is on a military uniform, and you can put a belt under this or you can hang a band from it. And when I'm referring to an epaulette, I am referring to this part of the uniform which starts at the neck and finishes at the end of the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. That puts it clearly now on the record in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the record perhaps reflect that what Mr. Zaric actually touched is not in the transcript was the part of his shoulder between his neck and the top of his arm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Zaric actually also said that while he was touching his shoulder from his neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we have clarified this point, we might add for the record that Mr. Zaric showed on his own shoulder where the epaulette was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, would you please answer the following question: What happened next that night, that is, on the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this conversation, I went back to bed and I fell asleep. Between 3.00 and 4.00 a.m., the telephone rang in my flat, and my wife woke me up once more and said: The phone's ringing. I picked up the receiver, and the duty officer from the command of the 4th Detachment, Mr. Miljenko Ugljesic was on the line. He said that he could hear gunfire at the eastern end of the town and in the direction of the public security station, and that the gunfire was becoming more frequent. I got up, or rather, I asked him whether he had informed Commander Antic of this. He said he was having difficulty reaching him, but he was trying to establish contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The eastern part of town, is that the part of town that the citizens of Samac commonly referred to as Donja Mahala?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That part of town is called Donja Mahala. That's where the customs house and the port on the River Sava are located.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After you received this information from the duty officer in the command of the 4th Detachment, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this, I made a phone call, or two phone calls, to two people from Donja Mahala, in order to try to find out whether they had any information. And to be quite honest, the shooting could be heard quite clearly, so that my wife and I went out onto the balcony and we could hear the sound of gunfire coming from the east. And I got Dragan Lujic on the phone, and Petar Karlovic, and also Joca Vukovic. So I spoke to three people, hastily, in order to find out what could be heard and what was happening in the part of the town where there was intense shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that they had noticed, because the streets were lighted up, that men in camouflage uniforms were moving along the streets, with hats on and with red berets, and that they were accompanied by policemen in blue uniforms and blue berets; that there was some shooting and that they were going from house to house looking for weapons, asking the citizens in that part of the town for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After you got this information, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this, I managed to call up Commander Antic on the phone, and he told me that we should meet as soon as possible in the command and that he was trying to establish communication with Mr. Stevan Nikolic, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, because he had received the same kind of information as I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say "received information," you mean Mr. Antic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean Mr. Antic. And as he was in the very centre of town, he said he had heard a loud explosion from the direction of the Municipal Assembly and the public security station and that he was concerned about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you, Mr. Zaric, go to the command, and who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in the command, I found Commander Antic there. He had arrived a little before me. I found Captain Savic and I found some people who were already in our patrols and who had reached the Samac textile industry and the command there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In the command, did you get any fresh information about events in the town?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our part of the patrol, which was not far from the silo and which was led by Mr. Mitar Sisic, who was there at the command already, they told us that some men had stopped at the crossroads. They got out of a truck. They were wearing camouflage uniforms. They didn't know who they were, and they set off in the direction of the Muslim cemetery and Donja Mahala, which belongs to the eastern part of the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody from the command establish to get in touch with the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one moment all the telephone lines broke up, but the commander managed to establish contact with the command of the 17th Tactical Group through the signals officers and the radio set that we had and that we used for the communication with the 17th Tactical Group. So Miljenko Ugljesic, the duty officer, established contact and Commander Nikolic briefed Commander Nikolic [as interpreted] about the situation, about the first pieces of information that we came by.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic -- Your Honours, it may help if we have a time for this. The information a moment ago was a phone call between 3.00 and 4.00. We haven't had a time yet for when Mr. Zaric went to the police station, sorry, the command, or when these other things happened. It would certainly help, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: One small clarification. Here we have, on page 43, it says: "Commander Nikolic briefed Commander Nikolic." It is obviously that he was referring to Mr. Antic who briefed Commander Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Commander Nikolic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's an obvious mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And also --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Also remember that Mr. Zaric referred to him going to the police station. I didn't understand what was the objection of my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. The Prosecution was just raising -- I think the Prosecution were asking that if he could estimate what time these events were happening, having woken up between 3.00 and 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
