utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what was the time when you -- when the first telephone call woke you up? That was when the duty officer from the 4th Detachment woke you up.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime between 3.00 and 4.00, but it was closer to 4.00. Between those times. I can't give you the exact minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I think the timing after -- when he reached the command, thereafter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I arrived at the command around 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I just have one little clarification too before your next question, Mr. Pisarevic. If I could just take you back to page 42, line 2. This is when Mr. Zaric, you mentioned that you got three people on the phone. And the first one is Dragan -- and here the surname is spelled L-u-j-i-c. I just want to confirm with you whether that is correct or whether it's the person you referred to earlier, the chief of police, Dragan Lukac. So I just want to clarify the spelling of the person's name on page 42, line 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Dragan Lujic, L-u-j-i-c, not Dragan Lukac, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when did Commander Radovan Antic manage to establish radio contact with Commander Nikolic, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was around 5.00, around the time when I came. It was either a quarter to 5.00 or a quarter past 5.00, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After this conversation with the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, what did your commander tell you? What did the commander of the 4th Detachment, Mr. Antic, tell you about the contents of that conversation that he had just had?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Antic gave me brief outlines of that conversation. He said that he informed Lieutenant Colonel that something was going on in the town of Samac, that there was gunfire from the eastern part of the town of Samac, and that we had received information from our members, members of the 4th Detachment, that in the Donja Mahala some people were moving about in camouflage uniforms and that there was also police in blue uniforms, in blue berets. That was the briefing that Commander Antic conveyed by telephone to Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, my question was: After that conversation, what did Mr. Radovan Antic tell you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that conversation, Commander Antic said that he had received an order from Commander Nikolic for him and myself to immediately go to Pelagicevo, to the command of the 17th Tactical Group, and to try and get there no later than 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you go there, you and Mr. Antic, commander of the 4th Detachment? Did you go to Pelagicevo, and when did you go?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after having received this information, Commander Antic and I left immediately for Pelagicevo. Commander Antic said to his deputy, Captain Jovo Savic, to stay in the command and to continue gathering intelligence and that he would try and contact him as soon as possible from Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did you go to Pelagicevo? What means of transportation did you use?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took my car to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you meet with anybody before you departed for Pelagicevo in front of the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the departure, as soon as we left our office, on the stairway, on its top part where these two rooms were, we came across Mr. Fadil Topcagic, who was rather upset. He wore a jacket. And when I asked him: Fadil, what's up? He told us briefly what had happened to him a few hours before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Topcagic actually tell you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told us that in the presence of Savo Savic, a policeman, and another man wearing a multicoloured uniform, he didn't know this man, but these two people came to his house, woke him up, and took him to Crkvina, and from there, he had to bring a group of people unknown to him to the public security station, and he had to tell them that this facility had now been taken [as interpreted] by these people and policemen unknown to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: One clarification here on page 47. Here it says, on line 8: "And that he had to tell them that this facility had now been taken." This doesn't make much sense. He actually told to Mr. Zaric and Mr. Antic that those facilities were taken by those specials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that can be corrected by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Topcagic forced to tell you that or did he tell you that of his own free will during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told us that of his own free will. He told us what had happened. He told us that he had gone to Crkvina, that one person there was wounded, that he came back on foot, and he came to the command. He seemed lost, although he is known as a very courageous man, from what I know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which route did you take to go to Pelagicevo, you and Mr. Antic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We drove along the right-hand side, via Crkvina and Kruskovo Polje and Gornja Slatina, because of the situation, we did not want to take the route on the left-hand side, via Grebnice, so we took a longer route, towards Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you remember the time when you arrived at the command of the 17th Tactical Group in Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived in some 50 minutes, so it could have been around 6.00 or 10 past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Zaric said a moment ago that: "We arrived in some 50 minutes." What did you talk about, you and Mr. Antic, during your journey to Pelagicevo, or did you sit quite silent? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember exactly. Obviously, we did not keep quiet. We discussed the situation and we were both very concerned. And it was in that mood that we arrived in Pelagicevo. But we did not voice any opinion as to what was really going on. We didn't voice any opinions about that in the car, that is. I can say that when people in multicoloured uniforms were mentioned, and knowing that had arrived, we knew that -- who these people were. We suspected who they were. But we were not a hundred per cent sure at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. If I may add something to this, Honourable Judge Lindholm. During my conversation with people from Donja Mahala, one of the members of the 4th Detachment, Mr. Petar Karlovic, told me: Simo, I can see some people in multicoloured uniforms. I don't know who they are. I'm afraid that it may be a sabotage group from the Republic of Croatia. He did not have a clue what this group was all about, who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Thank you very much. Who did you find in the command when you arrived in Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that almost the complete command staff was there, and they were all in the room that belonged to the Commander Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic. There was Chief Brajkovic, there was Mr. Makso Simeunovic, there was Sabrija, the chief of artillery, Milan Milicic, chief of the command office. There was a captain who was a member of the logistics of the 17th Tactical Group. I would say that the complete command staff of the 17th Tactical Group was there when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. What were you told by Commander Nikolic in the presence of all these people? What were his information -- what was his information about the developments in the city -- in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Nikolic told us something along these lines: He was informed sometime around midnight, or after midnight, rather, by telephone, and it was Mr. Blagoje Simic who informed him, that the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality had been established and they had decided to take over the most important facilities in town and to take over power in Samac. This was the briefest possible information that Commander Nikolic could have given us at that moment and that he actually gave us at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was yours and Mr. Radovan Antic's reaction to that information?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reacted in a very loud way, I would say. We were not very tactical in our reaction. But I remember that both Antic and myself asked the commander: So what does that mean? What is now the role of the 4th Detachment, and what kind of the Serbian government is now being introduced in the town given our clear task? The 4th Detachment was supposed to protect everybody who resided in this town and in this local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And after this reaction of yours, what did Commander Nikolic tell you, and did he issue any orders to you after that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told us that the message from him to Blagoje Simic was that he did not want to get involved in that part of politics. He warned him that he didn't want any bloodshed. And if some boundaries were stepped over, the army would place itself on the demarcation line. That is what he told us as having warned people about. But he also told us that the army would not get involved in that part of politics, especially when it comes to the introduction of some new form of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What orders did he issue to Mr. Radovan Antic, the commander of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that it had already been ordered to all the units on the strength of the 17th Tactical Group to be ready for combat, and he ordered Commander Antic, in front of everybody, to order their units higher combat readiness level and to inform his deputy from Pelagicevo that that should be done with an immediate effect. Mr. Antic carried out Commander Nikolic's order. He asked the duty signals officer in the 17th Tactical Group in Pelagicevo to call the command of the 4th Detachment in Samac, and he managed to get hold of his deputy, Jovo Savic, and he ordered him to call all commanders of squads and companies, and that these people should do their utmost to raise the combat readiness to the highest level but not to take any measures without further orders by the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did you and Commander Antic return to the command of the 4th Detachment in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been around 8.00 in the morning. It may have been around 8.00, and we had to do another detour on our way back in Hasici, a bridge had been blown up, so we couldn't go that way, so we had to cross some fields and we had to go through Milosevac and again through some fields to finally reach Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric literally said that people from Hasici had blown the bridge up. This is what we heard in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you've mentioned the village of Hasici and people from Hasici who had blown up a bridge. Who are residents of the village of Hasici? What is their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croats from Hasici blow up the bridge on that road?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had blown up the bridge. That bridge is not far from the exit from the village of Hasici towards Lugovi. Lugovi is a large farm or an agricultural combine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Because of that, because of the bridge having been blown up, you couldn't take the same route from Pelagicevo to Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to go towards Luzani and we had to take another detour. And since we were familiar with the area, we managed to get the command in Samac, having passed through Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Once you arrived in the command of the 4th Detachment in Samac, what did you find there? Were there any members of the 4th Detachment there? If so, how many had gathered there up to the moment when you returned around 8.00 on the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my estimate, there may have been about 40 to 50 people in front of the command. And when we arrived, they provided us with some information. They told us that there were three dead people in the town, that the police station had been taken, that the municipal building had been taken, that the silo had been taken, the radio station of Samac, that is, the memorial centre, the post office building, that the control of the bridge on the River Sava is now in the hands of the Serbs, and that the only manoeuvre area was towards the village of Prud and that the citizens were crossing over to that side across the bridge. And at the same time, we noticed a number of passenger cars moving towards Crkvina, in the depth of the territory, carrying families, towards the southern part of Samac. There was a state of chaos in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information as to what was going on in the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We obtained information about that sometime around 10.00 or 11.00, a group of armed Muslims had taken some of the main points in the town, not far from the department store, not far from the mosque, not far from the park and the hotel, and we also heard that they were trying to establish control over part of the bridge leading towards the village of Prud and onwards towards Odzak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but a while ago Mr. Zaric told us that -- it's on page 52, line -- well, let's start on line 15, the last word: "And at the same time, we noticed a number of passenger cars moving towards Crkvina, in the depth of the territory, carrying families, towards the southern part of Samac." Can you be a bit more precise on that point? Who were leaving, and what did they perhaps meet when they crossed the southern part or the southern border of the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the first day, that is, on the 17th of April, there was movement towards the southern part of the municipality and there was also movement towards the village of Prud, across the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That's in another direction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: You were telling us that you saw people leaving in passenger cars towards the south. And if I understand the geography correctly, Prud is to the west and not to the south. So if you stick to what you told us, watching people going in passenger cars towards the south, crossing, I assume, the border of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, who were those people, and what do you think they expected to meet when crossing the border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not mean that -- when I said that they were driving towards the south, I did not mean that they were crossing the border, that you're asking me about. I only know that they were moving in that direction. And when they're southbound, they can enter Crkvina or Skaric, or they can take some routes to get to Hasici 1 or Hasici 2. They can reach Hrvatska Tisina. So this part of the southern part of the municipality had different routes, different roads. I did not have the time to see who was riding in those cars, what families were those. But I suppose that people wanted to move out of the town in the largest possible numbers, because the stories had already started circulating. And as for the western part, as for Prud, according to the information that we have subsequently obtained, it was mostly Croats who left in that direction, and for the most part Muslim families, according to the information that we managed to obtain from the people who had a better view of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, people who headed south, to the southern part of the municipality of Samac, you saw them, didn't you? Did you recognise in those cars -- could you say what ethnic group the passengers in those cars belonged? Were only Serbs leaving or was it Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They belonged to all three groups. In the beginning, there were not any serious checkpoints there on the ground. So that it was obvious that one could get through, especially if one took some round about roads, if one avoided the main highway. And those who were familiar with the area could very easily get through and get out without coming across a checkpoint such as, for instance, the one in Crkvina, where Dragan Lukac fetched up, where he was arrested and then turned back. There were a number of other exits which could be taken to get out and move to Gradacac and then Croat and Serb villages in the southern part of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I was about to ask you this thing about Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Before you do, maybe, Mr. Pisarevic: I'm just a little bit confused by the last answer, Mr. Zaric, to judge -- no. To Mr. Pisarevic, where, with respect to his question, which was -- this is line 16, page 54: "Did you recognise in those cars -- could you say what ethnic group the passengers in those cars belonged? Were they only Serbs or was it Croats or Muslims?" And your answer that we have here on line 19 is they belonged to all three ethnic groups. Now, my confusion is because in your earlier answer to Judge Lindholm with respect to: Did you know who was riding in those cars? You say, on page 54, lines 5 and 6: "I did not have the time to see who was riding in those cars, what families were those." So I'd just like a little bit of clarification whether you did see the people or not, as the case might be, in those cars travelling south towards Crkvina and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to be quite honest, Your Honour, I could see some of the limos and I could see drivers in them. But a vast number passed by and I only managed to register them from looking from above, from an upper floor, without being able to ascertain who was in those cars. But when I said that I saw people belonging to other ethnic groups -- for instance, I remember a Roma, Mr. Roma. I can't remember his last name -- whom I knew very well, worked for the social auditing service, who is a Muslim, and who with his family went in that direction, and I know that later on he went to Gradacac and had no problems there at all. I remember, for instance, that Anto, who was the president of the Executive Board, also went through with his family and moved on towards his village, but I cannot say that I saw everybody else. So when I said this, I merely assumed that there were also people belonging to other ethnic groups, but I simply -- that I saw everybody, it would be too pretentious on my part to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And this exodus of people towards the southern part of the municipality, did it take the whole of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost the whole of the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you did not see, you merely heard, that people were crossing the bridge across the Bosna.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning I heard that. Later on, I saw that, because later on I went out to bordering areas, in the adjacent area, when these border areas were taken, the traffic was not stopped, and there was no control of the vehicles wanting to cross the bridge across the Bosna. And it lasted until 1800 hours, when the exchange of fire started.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me this: Which is the municipality adjacent to the municipality of Samac on the southern -- along its southern borders?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the municipality of Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In the command of the 4th Detachment, Mr. Zaric, did you, in the course of that day, receive any other orders from the command of the 17th Tactical Group? Are you aware of any such orders?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I merely wish to say that when we arrived in the command, Commander Antic had a conversation with Commander Nikolic, during which he briefed him about the latest developments and a number of those killed. I told you that we had information that three had been killed, two Croats and one Serb. That certain facilities had been taken and about what had been going on in the town. At that point, Commander Nikolic ordered Commander Antic to raise the 4th Detachment and take the boundary areas, practically, the right bank of the Bosna, from where the town begins, and that is from the brick works, ending with its mouth into the Sava River, and to take the right bank of the dike alongside the Sava River, on the border with Republic of Croatia from the port which is not far away on the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When was that order issued?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been sometime around 9.00, straight away, almost immediately on our return, because there was this conversation and it was around 9.00 that this issue was carried to the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How many men reported to the command of the 4th Detachment at around 9.00? How many men were there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, much less than we were expecting. However, the situation simply caught almost all of us unaware. Members of the 4th Detachment, of the 1st and the 2nd and the 3rd ethnicity [Realtime transcript read in error "of necessity"] looked after their families first, to take them out or to protect them, and a number of members turned up and responded to the summons issued by the messenger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have a misunderstanding here in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric has members of the 4th Detachment, of the 1st and the 2nd, and the 3rd nationality, meaning of all three nationalities. The way it is in the transcript would suggest numbers of 1st Detachment, 2nd and 3rd Detachments. He wasn't referring to other detachments at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, I think it's better to go over that to make it clear as to what he meant.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, interpreter's comment. The word was to be "ethnicity," not "necessity."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, will you tell us: When you spoke about the response of the members of the 4th Detachment and whether they came to the command, did you say that all three ethnic groups which were there responded or will you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the members of the 4th Detachment, and I mentioned men, that is, members of the 4th Detachment of all three ethnicities, meaning Croats, Muslims, and Serbs. We did not respond all that diligently, not that they didn't want to, but because the situation was such that -- not respond en masse to those earlier summons carried by messengers, as requested by commanders of companies and platoons. Because they simply wanted to look after their families first, to take them out or protect them, so that of the total number, and I told you here that the 4th Detachment was about 450 strong, in the beginning, when we started carrying out this task, we were perhaps, when we set off into this action, we were perhaps between 50 and 70. So that to my mind, it wasn't a particularly encouraging figure. However, the number increased as the time went by and people began to come in. And as they came in, we who were responsible for establishing this defence line, we distributed, together with commanders of individual units, we deployed those men as specified by the orders that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that some members of the 4th Detachment were unable to reach the command of the 4th Detachment because of the situation in the town?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is one of the reasons, and that is why I'm talking about a confusion about something that happened when the war broke out, and we were all rather, how shall I say, pioneers, or rather, we came from peaceful institutions when it comes to understanding to what terrible things could happen to us. That is, none of us had any wartime experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, now that you used the word "pioneers," here, as Mr. Lazarevic suggests to me, when that word is used, it may mean something else, so will you please tell us: What did you mean by this, when you said we were pioneers?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of us had any experience in this type of war which befell us. That is what I meant. When I said "pioneers," I meant children who had barely started school and acquiring first basic knowledge. I tried to put it slightly hypothetically, but that is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As said by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And how long did this action of taking the boundary areas around the town of Samac last?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have lasted, I'd say, until about 1500 or 1600 hours. That is, we needed several hours to take the boundary areas to mark the basic positions which in our opinion would suffice to prevent any surprise attack or incursion of enemy forces from Prud or the Republic of Croatia, either across the bridge or perhaps some assault by using the stream, that is, the River Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When the 4th Detachment was taken out to those boundary areas, to those defence lines, were there any armed conflicts with the citizens?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these boundary areas where we were, there were no excesses of that type, nor was there any need for us to exchange either infantry or any other fire in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And was there any action in the town of Samac, I mean artillery or any other, on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that 17th, one could hear very frequent shots. We practically did not go deep into the town, especially after we learned -- after we had learned that there were groups of armed individuals in some parts of the town which were ready and prepared to offer armed resistance because they had been observed with armament.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Members of the 4th Detachment who were taken out to that defence line, to those dikes on the right bank of the Bosna and the right bank of the Sava, did they stay on those positions that night?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They stayed there the whole night. And we insisted in particular both the commander and I, and we were the ones who visited that line. Most -- we insisted that the whole night had to be spent there until we ensured some shifts, because those were very early hours. And I must say that people carried out that part of their task very patiently and very conscientiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you do something so that the members of the 4th Detachment who were on that defence line, that is, on the dikes, could recognise each other? Did you do something in that regard?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received this order from the command of the 17th Tactical Group. They told army members who were along combat lines were to have a uniform patch, and it was suggested to find it and to put on a white ribbon, with a view to carrying out this order, I went to a shop in the afternoon, which was open in the town, and the shop steward was Esad Porobic. It was a textile shop. And I got from him a roll of white cloth. I signed a document duly, saying that we needed it, gave him a piece of paper saying that I had taken it, and I took this roll to the command so that they could -- so that this cloth could be cut into ribbons 20 by 2 centimetres, so that in the evening people could put it on, use it as markings, all the people who were -- who held combat lines or rather, defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you yourself, together with somebody else, visited the dikes along Bosna and Sava during the night between the 17th and the 18th of April. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: And if I can recollect the geography of the town of Bosanski Samac in a right way, you couldn't get there unless you went either swimming along the rivers or walking along the dikes, but rather, you went through the city of Bosanski Samac, didn't you? Yes or no. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within that context, I did not go through the town in the evening of the 17th. But on the 18th, I could do it, and I did it, in a car, without any problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. My next question is: You said that your soldiers, or the members of the 4th Detachment, they were wearing white armbands on their left-hand shoulder, which you could recognise and see during the night between the 17th and the 18th of April. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when those ribbons were made, they were distributed to -- through a messenger. The messenger took it to company and platoon commanders and company and platoon commanders then distributed them amongst their shoulders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: No. My question was: How did you get there, to the dikes of the Bosna and the Sava River? You said you made it by car.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 18th, I could easily get there by car. In the evening of the 17th, I walked right along the dike, like all the other soldiers, and I moved from one soldier to the other, moving quite close to the dike, because these dikes are on the outskirts of the town of Samac. I didn't have to go through the residential area to reach the dikes. I mean a boundary area of the town without any residences, and therefore it was not difficult for me to move from one soldier to the other, from one commander to the other, to see what was the situation and to show them that we from the command were near them and with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes, but as all of us know, the distance between the dike along the Sava River and the buildings in the town is something between 20 and 50 metres. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are. Maybe even less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. And all of us know that those people in camouflage uniforms were moving around vital buildings, very close to the Sava River and dike along it. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, except for the SUP building, no other building is close enough. There is only the bridge across the Sava, but we got to that bridge only after three days. And other vital facilities are in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes, but the SUP building is very close to the dike along the Sava River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SUP building is, and that's what I said. That is the only vital building which is in the immediate vicinity of the Sava River bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes. And did you see people in those multicoloured or camouflage uniforms around the SUP building between the 17th and the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw them on the 18th of April, in the afternoon. I saw them live, because that was the first time that I went to the public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll take our break and continue at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to introduce a document. This is our number from pre-trial PDB 12/4. The document has been disclosed to the Prosecution. I believe that the members of the Chamber have it before them. And I also see that Mr. Zaric has it before him. This is the records of the interrogation of the witness before the military court in Orasje. This was compiled by Ivo Lukac, the investigating judge, in the proceedings conducted against Simo Zaric for the crime of armed rebellion and aggravated crimes against civilians from Article 102 in connection with article 102, paragraph 2, and Article 132 of the criminal law adopted from the Former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The records is dated 21st of July, 1994. The witness, in the proceedings, was Esad Dulovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, could you please look at page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I understand Mr. Pisarevic is attempting to tender this document, but is that what's happening at the moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Well, he wants to discuss it with the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't object to him discussing with -- I just notify the Trial Chamber now, the Prosecution will question the relevance of the document. Maybe Mr. Pisarevic can make it relevant. The Prosecution has certainly seen many of these types of documents in relation to a lot of the witnesses who have already been called, but of course we don't attempt to tender any of these into evidence. So we just raise the question before he goes any further, please make this relevant to the proceedings in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think the counsel can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution had a couple of months, and if I may say, they have this documents in their possession for a couple of years. They were informed that we will use this document in the course of examination of Mr. Zaric and that we would like to present this document into evidence, well, at least for a few months, and it was disclosed to the Prosecution in our pre-trial brief. But the source of this document is the Prosecution. They provided us with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think what the Prosecution are asking is the relevance of this document to the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We are now at the topic of white ribbons, and Mr. Zaric has just testified that he went to the shop, that he took a quantity, and this is what the document is about, because this witness who testified, Mr. Porobic, was actually the salesman who gave the white ribbons to Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, are you on page 2 of this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: First of all let me ask you: Do you know Mr. Esad Porobic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did he reside? Where did Mr. Esad Porobic reside in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He resided in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This gentleman, Mr. Porobic, what was his profession? Where did he work?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a highly qualified salesman, and I worked together with him in the same company for seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the fourth paragraph, line 5. Could you please read this sentence.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kindly tell me what were the -- what are the first words of this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: "He was --"

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "He was a very sociable and communicative person. He often helped people whenever he had the chance to do that. Before the occupation, one couldn't notice anything about his person that would point to the fact that he was a negative person, in terms of his participation or preparation of an armed rebellion."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would kindly ask you to read the part starting with the following words: "At that time I had a meeting with the defendant Simo Zaric."

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At that time, I had a meeting with the defendant Simo Zaric. That was when Simo Zaric came with another man to my shop. I believe that this was after my working hours. He asked me to deliver a certain quantity of cloth because he needed that cloth for some insignia for the troops in the units. The defendant treated me with respect. Moreover, he left a written document with me for the delivery of the goods."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And can you please read the part starting with: "In his behaviour," the same paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "As for his behaviour, or a violent attitude towards non-Serbian population of Bosanski Samac, I wouldn't be able to state anything, given the --"

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I do object to this. The relevance we were told was that this is somehow corroborative of Mr. Zaric's evidence that it was he who purchased the ribbons. Okay. For whatever weight this document can be given to support his evidence to that, fine. We're not going to worry too much about that. But this seems to be trying to get character evidence in through the back door, through a document that was apparently taken in a Croatian type of court. We do object to that. And in any event, the document speaks for itself. I don't know why it's being read onto the record. It speaks for itself if it's going to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber doesn't see any objectionable reason why it can't be received into evidence except that perhaps what you point out is that there is no need to read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because what --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was just one more part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. If you want to tender it, you go ahead with that, and then you simply discuss what it shows. Because we can all read the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no reason for me to go on reading this document, because, as has been stated, it speaks for itself. I would only like to ask Mr. Zaric the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Has this document been signed by the witness, Esad Porobic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And the signature of the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I know this judge very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that proceedings were initiated before the military court of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in Orasje?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that only at the moment when it appeared as an item of the agenda before this Trial Chamber, when my provisional release was discussed, and that was the first time when I learned that I had been condemned to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it please be given a number for this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D51/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let me ask the Prosecution. I thought they were not objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. It's a matter of weight. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So it's D51/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, during the day of the 17th of April, did you have a telephone call? If so, who called you, and what did you discuss with that person?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a telephone call during the 17th of April, around noon, and it was Mr. Ibrahim Salkic who called me. His nickname is Ibela.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you talk about with Mr. Salkic when he called you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ibrahim Salkic called me and told me that he and other Muslims who were in the centre of town, under arms, that they wanted to lay down their weapons, but he wanted to talk about that before and be given the word by Mr. Stevan Nikolic, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group. He asked me whether I could give him the number for this person to call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you give him the number?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did give him the telephone number, and Mr. Salkic, according to the information that I subsequently obtained, called Commander Nikolic and talked to him, and all the weapons that he and his group of Muslims had at their disposal at several points in town was handed over to the public security station in Samac rather than to the members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric. On that day, that is, the 17th of April, did you receive information about the call for help that Mr. Salkic and Mr. Suljic sent to the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Antic and I returned from Pelagicevo, the duty officer in our communications centre, Mr. Miljenko Ugljesic, informed us that during the communications means, he intercepted a conversation between Namik Suljic and Ibrahim Salkic, Ibela, and certain people from the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian Defence Council from Prud. Apparently they asked them to deliver on their promise. That was to extend them help in order to take the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Commander Nikolic issue any other orders on that day, on the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that not for a moment did we underestimate the information that we had received, and that is that help was asked from the Republic of Croatia and the HVO from Prud. This message was conveyed to the commander, and we told him that a group of armed men were to be found in the town. Commander Nikolic then said that he would issue an order through the competent commander to send two BOVs and armoured vehicles to the town. The abbreviation is BOV. That is the CAV or the armoured combat vehicle, which has four barrels, two smaller ones and two bigger ones [as interpreted]. This is basically an anti-aircraft piece of equipment. He said he was going to send these pieces of weaponry to act as prevention against any possible attacks on the suburban areas, and also to somehow be a signal to the forces in the town that it would be dangerous for them to engage in any armed conflict. So when these two CAVs appeared, and at the beginning they just cruised the streets of the town, Mr. Salkic called and did what I have just spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This CAV, how many barrels did it have?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This CAV has one barrel and two smaller barrels underneath, but we call it a one-barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, the record is wrong. It reads: Four barrels.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It has three barrels. It has one bigger one and two smaller barrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer the following question: On the day of the 17th of April, did Commander Nikolic issue any other orders to the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we received information that the weapons from the centre of the town, from which there was the biggest threat to the entire town, that this had been handed over, Commander Nikolic issued an order to the following effect: On the suburban areas, where the members of the 4th Detachment were deployed, they were to make rounds of the closest houses with a group of soldiers and ask for all the illegal weapons to be handed over in order to secure the protection of the unit members who were on the dike on the right bank of the River Sava and on the right river bank of the River Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the order of Commander Antic on the way the illegal weapons were to be collected?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Antic issued an order to a small group that was in patrol on the 17th, in the afternoon, to approach every house along the dike, not to enter any of the houses, not to carry out any search, to ask for weapons if the people had any illegal weapons, and they were strictly forbidden from entering any house or carrying out any search. This was an express order and it was also ordered that the collected weapons should be delivered to a certain place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, this action of collecting military weapons from the citizens of Samac, did it continue on the 18th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the majority of this task was indeed carried out on the 18th of April, because on the 17th of April, we only had two hours before the night fell, so that this action of the collection of weapons, especially when it comes to the 4th Detachment, and in that area, was carried out on the 18th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: While this action was being carried out in order to collect military weapons from citizens, did you, Mr. Zaric, have any concrete tasks and duties?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Honourable Chamber: What were your duties? What was your role in that action? And who assigned you that role? Who gave you your orders on that day?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, 1992, Commander Antic issued an order to two groups, consisting of eight to ten men each. According to that order, in the part of the town that we called the fourth quarter, or the fourth neighbourhood, they were supposed to collect the illegal weapons from citizens, and again he pointed to the fact that this had to be done in a humane manner, that no searches were to be done, that this should be done in a conversation with the fellow citizens, and then that finally the collected weapons should be taken to the Territorial Defence staff. As for me personally, I remember it well. At the meeting of the command, so to me personally and to Mr. Tadic, he ordered that, in addition to the tasks that we already had, I on the defence line and Mr. Tadic, already on the 18th, had two tasks. One was in connection with the transfer of the command to another place for security reasons, and he also had a task to organise a kitchen, a field kitchen. But he told the two of us that we should meet from time to time in the area where the action was under way and that the two of us should make sure that his orders were obeyed to the last letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There is one thing missing in the transcript. Mr. Zaric had mentioned the fourth quarter of the town, and I don't see this in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought he had said that, line 9, I think: "According to that order, in the part of the town that we called the fourth quarter, or the fourth neighbourhood." That is covered. We can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. I heard it twice, so maybe ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was your role to monitor, to control the situation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the context that I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, tell us: How did you control the collection of weapons and the manner in which this activity was carried out?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My primary task was to constantly tour the defence line. On the 18th, in the morning, I was given a driver, Toso Tutnjevic, also known as Toso, and a car. They were put at my disposal. And in view of the route we followed and my wish to reach as many places as possible in order to monitor the security of the line, and in order to carry out my task, I moved by vehicle with Mr. Tutnjevic. We would come to a street, stop. I would look to see what was happening and then we would go to another part of town or to the line, and then go back, in order to see how this part of the task was being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you know whether the members of the 4th Detachment entered citizens' houses and flats?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know of a single case when a member of the 4th Detachment entered anyone's home and carried out any sort of search or anything similar that might cause dissatisfaction among citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any cases of use of force or threats against citizens by members of the 4th Detachment during the action of collecting weapons?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard anything like that, either during the war or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were the soldiers who participated in collecting the weapons accompanied or escorted by any kind of armoured vehicle; and if they were, what kind of vehicle was it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the two armoured combat vehicles I have just mentioned, from the 17th, which came during the day. And on the following day, the same two vehicles arrived, but this time they escorted the group that went from street to street, and they put the weapons they had collected into a part of this vehicle, where weapons could be left without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did this vehicle resemble a tank at all?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's nothing like a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did any tanks arrive in Bosanski Samac on the 17th and 18th April?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the members of the 4th Detachment who participated in collecting weapons in the fourth quarter, were there any other persons or members of any other units?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of the fourth quarter, there were members of no other units, apart from the members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, during your control of the collection of weapons, were you in Pere Bosica Street, in front of the house of Sabrija Dagovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, were you in the vicinity of Sabrija Dagovic's house?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was on Djure Djakovica Street which is not far and which crosses Pere Bosica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, on that day, the 18th of April, 1992, were you at any moment accompanied by Mr. Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not together for a single moment, except that I saw Mr. Tadic passing by in a street near the fire brigade headquarters, but we never walked together, not for a single moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did this action of collecting weapons from citizens end?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It ended on the 18th, in the afternoon, the 18th of April, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what was done with these weapons that were collected?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these weapons were taken to the building of the Territorial Defence, which is opposite the public security station, and they were left in a warehouse or a depot which had been used to store weapons previously, except that this time the weapons were thrown in haphazardly rather than being neatly stacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know anything as to how many weapons the members of the 4th Detachment collected in the fourth quarter? Do you know the number of weapons?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't enter the depot, but I was told --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the fourth quarter, I think the 4th Detachment found between 250 and 300 barrels of various kinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Counsel, before we go forward, I would like to ask Mr. Zaric -- it's about his answer on page 74, line 21. He, according to the transcript, said: "In the area of the fourth quarter there were members of no other units, apart from the members of the 4th Detachment." This is a very ambiguous answer, because it refers only to the fourth quarter of the town of Bosanski Samac. Were there perhaps other units moving around in other parts of the town collecting weapons, and how were they composed? Were also those groups members of the 4th Detachment only, or were there other persons involved in that collecting of weapons? Could you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my next question, which I was just beginning to put, was the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know who was collecting weapons in the remaining part of town, that is, in the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd quarters of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know about this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the first evening, between the 16th and the 17th, in the area of Donja Mahala, a complete search was made by the specials and the Serbian police which entered, and they completed that part of the task in the second and third quarters as well. So that we did not even enter those areas. And the only reason we got this information that they had passed through that part of the town was that a lot of unpleasant situations had arisen, and for this reason it was not advisable for us to go and repeat our activity in the areas where they had already been.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of unpleasant situations had arisen? What did these people do? What did you hear? When did you hear this about the specials?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard a part of this very soon, on the 18th. They entered houses, conducted searches, looked for weapons; not in every house, but in most houses. They confiscated weapons, even from members of the 4th Detachment who had proper documents. They took legally owned weapons, including hunting rifles, from citizens who had proper licences. So that their attitude when confiscating weapons was what I have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when did you learn that the police and the Specials, during the searches, arrested citizens of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stories about that reached us on the 17th. I didn't see that personally, but I got some information from some members of the 4th Detachment who had succeeded in coming to our area, and we heard that people were being arrested, that their weapons were being taken away, and I also received information on members of the 4th Detachment who had been arrested and who were already in the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you tell anyone about what you learned?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who did you inform?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I immediately informed Mr. Makso Simeunovic about that chaotic situation, and he immediately informed the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, so that what was happening in the town of Samac, without control, was known by my Superior Command in the 17th Tactical Group from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you also inform them that members of the 4th Detachment had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I spoke to the commander personally, Commander Nikolic, because he happened to be there in the command. And I said to him I could not comprehend the behaviour of the Serbian policemen and the Specials, that they had no criteria, and that they had arrested, among others, a number of members of the 4th Detachment who had proper licences, legitimate documents, and who had weapons as members of the 4th Detachment of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I have a question here. Mr. Zaric, you told us a while ago that you had, so to say, a channel of information between you yourself, your commander, Mr. Antic, and the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic. What about channels of information between you, as representing the military part of what was going on, and the municipal authorities in the town of Samac, taking into account that the town of Samac is a rather small community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My only communication which I maintained with the military command in Pelagicevo was through the radio equipment we had in the command of the 4th Detachment, which means that if I needed to transmit anything to my superior officer, Makso Simeunovic, or the commander, I had to go to the command of the 4th Detachment, and from there, ask for a communications link and ask to speak to them. I had no other way of establishing contact, and I did not contact with the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. Apparently I didn't make myself clear enough. I'm not interested in by which means you established contact between you yourself and the commander of the 17th Tactical Group. What I'm interested in, whether any kind of channels of information as between you and the municipal authorities in the town of Bosanski Samac, civilian authorities. Can you please reply to that question, shortly, and not going astray.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no information and no connections with the municipal authorities on the 17th and the 18th, directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Do you know - perhaps this is just a suggestion - that anybody else had, so to say, communication with the civil -- the municipal authorities in the town of Bosanski Samac about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the command of the 4th Detachment, I know that no one from the command of the 4th Detachment had any communication with the authorities in Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Commander Nikolic say he would do for the members of the 4th Detachment to be released?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he would intervene right away and that he would inform us about the outcome of his talks. And when he said he would intervene, he was referring to Mr. Todorovic, who was the chief of the public security station. After informing Commander Nikolic about an hour later, I received information that he had talked with Mr. Blagoje Simic and with Mr. Stevan Todorovic, that he had informed them of this fact, that is, that weapons had been confiscated from members of the 4th Detachment and that they had been arrested, and he asked that these people be released. And he said that I, as the assistant commander for security, would go to the public security station to collect these men and to see that they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did Commander Nikolic order you to go to the police station in Bosanski Samac and to take over the members of the 4th Detachment who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did you take over the members of the 4th Detachment at the police station in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the police station in Bosanski Samac on the 18th, in the early evening, and then on the following day, because during the night some other members had also been arrested, I went there and I reported to the duty officer, Ilija Vukojevic. I said I had arrived and that I wanted to talk to the chief of the station in order to have the members of the 4th Detachment who were detained there released.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you manage to talk to Mr. Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Stevan Todorovic was upstairs, in one of the offices, with a team I didn't know, and he said: Brother Serb, you have arrived. I didn't like this very much, but I said I was there pursuant to his conversation with my commander and that I was there because the members of the 4th Detachment were to be released and their weapons returned to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And were the members of the 4th Detachment released, and can you recall some names, if you can?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that on that occasion, in the public security station there were several members of the 4th Detachment. One of them was Tadija Brandic, who was an ethnic Croat and who was also a platoon leader in the 4th Detachment, which is very characteristic. Then there was Muharem Kapetanovic, also known as Sora [phoen], a Muslim. There was Hajrudin Seljakovic, also known as Mrki. There was Mustafa Omeranovic, Mujaga also known as Mustafa. There was Asim Avdic and there was Marko Filipovic, whom they had arrested in the course of the night, and on the following day, on the 19th, I had to go back to get him out. That's why I said I went to collect another one on the 19th. So these five or six men were released from the public security station, but Mr. Todorovic did not return their weapons. Their weapons were not returned to them at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, where in the police station were these people detained?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to confess: I don't know where they were detained. When I said that I had come to collect these members of the 4th Detachment, he asked me who are these men from the 4th Detachment, and I said: Well, I don't know who you have here in the public security station. And he sent me to Vukojevic, the duty officer, who had in front of him a book, where they recorded who was detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did the duty officer, Ilija Vukojevic, do so that these members of the 4th Detachment would be released?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When in that logbook I saw 30 or 40 names, and I found the names I have just mentioned, I said to Mr. Vukojevic: These are the men who should be released, and I agreed on this with Chief Stevo. Then Mr. Vukojevic - whose chief I had been before, he was an older professional policeman - he said: Mr. Zaric, I trust you, but I have to ask my chief once more whether I have to release these men. So he called Stevo again, Stevo Todorovic, the chief, from the duty officer's room, and when he said it was all right, then he brought these men into the corridor and I apologised to these men because they had found themselves in this situation, and then they went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did the members of the 4th Detachment who were there, had they been beaten while they were detained in the police station? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Almost all of them were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did you find this out?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I saw them. I saw the bruises on Mr. Abdic and on Mr. Mrki, that is, Hajrudin Seljakovic, also known as Mrki. I saw bruises on Mr. Tadija, Mujaga Omeranovic was my brother-in-law, and a platoon leader, and he was the one who had been beaten the worst and who had the worst bruises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, can we break here? There are just two matters we want to discuss. We can continue with Mr. Zaric tomorrow. The Trial Chamber has been informed that Mr. Marko Tubakovic has arrived today, and the Trial Chamber has decided that we shall hear him tomorrow. We will begin with him, so that he can be returned. When we are through with him, then we continue with Mr. Zaric. And the other matter is that on Friday, the Trial Chamber intends to sit for one and a half hours in the afternoon, starting at 1445 hours, to allow the interpreters and the crew to move their equipment. So we shall sit in the afternoon as well, from 1445 to 1615 hours, on Friday. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, what Your Honours, what you've just said in relation to Mr. Tubakovic may present the Prosecution with some difficulty. It is this: I'm co-counsel in another case, and tomorrow afternoon I have a meeting arranged with a German general who is the expert witness in the other case, which I'm trying to do because it's the only time he can come in the next few months between 1.30 and about a quarter to 4.00, or 4.15, when we had the break, and I'm the person who has been assigned to do Mr. Tubakovic. And Mr. Di Fazio and Mr. Weiner were going to sit in for me for Mr. Zaric while I was interviewing the general, who is a military expert. I was wondering if it would be possible for Mr. Tubakovic to give his evidence in the latter part of the afternoon. I only say this because I've only found this out right now, and I reorganised matters with the German general this morning on the basis that Mr. Zaric was coming today, or sorry, Mr. Zaric would be still giving his evidence tomorrow. It just will present us with some difficulty in someone else getting on top of Mr. Tubakovic's evidence, which I was the person who had him before in Belgrade. But that's all. If possibly he could give it after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. The proceedings have priority because of the problems that we face in these proceedings. So we'll begin with Mr. Tubakovic and then you can readjust your meeting with the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can't, because the expert -- the expert is coming in -- I spoke to him this morning. He was going to come on the night train and come in the morning, but I said: No, no. Because Mr. Zaric is scheduled to give his evidence, Mr. Di Fazio and Mr. Weiner will do it. And he has to catch a train -- a plane at 7.00 p.m. He will only be in The Hague between about 1.00, if then -- he's getting here at midday and he'll be leaving by about a quarter past 4.00 to catch his plane. That's the only time we have been able to arrange a meeting with this general for several months, because he's all over the place. It's just a clash which I couldn't see coming with Mr. Tubakovic until this moment. That's the real difficulty we have with that. I wouldn't ask, but it's just it's a meeting that's been arranged for several months, and I've only just found this out this minute. If I had known yesterday I would have asked him to catch the night train, but it's too late now. He's actually -- he was actually the commander of NATO forces in Bosnia. He's -- it's very difficult to get him here. That's the difficulty. Mr. Withopf --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. You can see the problems we all face in these matters. But proceedings have priority, and we just have to hear this witness so that he doesn't stay a day longer. Yes. We have to finish him tomorrow. Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would only like to inform you that Mr. Tubakovic set out yesterday from Bosanski Samac. He arrived today. And my colleague Mr. Lazarevic and I have not seen him at all. The witness was scheduled as a deposition witness, and I think that we would need at least a day and that Mr. Tubakovic could testify on Friday, because we need to proof him at least a little bit, prepare him in a way for his testimony. So we would kindly ask you, if at all possible, to allow this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. You've come to the rescue of Mr. Re, which I'm sure Mr. Re is very grateful. In view of your requirement to have a chat with Mr. Tubakovic, then we will hear him on Friday, since we are sitting the whole day. We hope that we should be able to complete him so that he can go back. So we'll adjourn now and continue our proceedings tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of May 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
